Five Pro Leagues Push States to Ban Abusive Bettors

Published September 16, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

The NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL, and MLS, together with their players' associations, sent a joint letter to state gaming regulators this week asking for tougher, coordinated rules against bettors who threaten or harass athletes, coaches, officials, and their families over betting outcomes.

What the leagues are asking for

The letter calls for mandatory lifetime betting bans for bettors verified to have made threatening or harassing contact, along with cross-state exclusion lists that would automatically apply a ban across every state where a bettor is caught, rather than leaving enforcement isolated to a single jurisdiction. The leagues also asked for a streamlined process letting them submit evidence of abuse directly to regulators, and for sportsbooks to build out account-monitoring and suspension protocols tied to that evidence. "Threatening the safety of an athlete or their family members over a sports bet crosses a bright ethical and criminal line," the leagues said in their joint statement.

Where enforcement already exists

A small number of states — Ohio, West Virginia, Louisiana, and Wyoming — already operate some form of exclusion list targeting bettors for this kind of conduct, but those lists currently apply only within each state's own borders. Separately, some operators have moved on their own: Fanatics Sportsbook and BetMGM have each rolled out abuse-detection tools that monitor social media and in-app messaging for threatening contact directed at athletes, according to the leagues' letter.

Why it matters to a US bettor

Athlete harassment tied to prop bets and in-game performance has become a recurring storyline as player-prop betting has grown, and this letter is the clearest sign yet that the leagues want state regulators — not just individual sportsbooks — to own the enforcement response. If states adopt a shared, cross-jurisdiction exclusion list, it would mark a meaningful shift from today's patchwork, where a bettor banned in one state for this kind of conduct can typically still bet freely in another. For the overwhelming majority of bettors who never come close to this line, the practical effect would likely be invisible — but it signals regulators may take a harder look at account-level monitoring more broadly as this push moves forward.
